title: Perennial grain crops
bottleneck: Annual grains require yearly tillage, planting, and fertilization — an ecological treadmill — while perennial grains like Kernza promise continuous cover, deep roots, and minimal inputs. But after decades of breeding, perennial yields remain a fraction of annuals: the plant partitions energy to roots and survival rather than grain, and the yield gap hasn't closed fast enough to convince farmers to switch.
why_it_blocks: Perennial agriculture could end the erosion and input treadmill of annual cropping. Without competitive yields, it stays an ecological ideal, not a farming system. Perennial agriculture could end the erosion and input treadmill of annual cropping - if yields ever compete.
current_state: Kernza is commercialized at small scale; yields are roughly a quarter of annual wheat with slow improvement.
